articleTitle: The role of space charge in the theory of solid-dielectric breakdown
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The first theory for low temperature electrical breakdown in solids was given by Zener[1] who calculated the field strength at which quantum mechanical tunneling from valence to conduction levels should become significantly large. This criterion for breakdown would clearly produce conditions leading to failure of insulating properties, but the critical fields calculated in this way are an order of magnitude larger than experimental breakdown strengths.

articleTitle: Conclusions
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The results presented above show that in addition to yielding conductive materials at very low additive content, reticulate doping of polymers with conductive CT complexes makes it possible to obtain materials of very low, positive or even negative, temperature coefficient of conductivity. Interesting possibilities of modification of the specific conductivity and of its thermal coefficient by annealing are now being investigated in our laboratory.

articleTitle: Electrical behaviour and structure of water trees in relation to their propagation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: In order to understand the propagation mechanisms of water trees it is essential to have a good knowledge of their microscopic structure. The question of the nature of the damage undergone by the polymer in water treeing has been much debated for a long time. Only recently, some authors assert that a water tree is made of channels [1], some others report that only microcavities have been observed [2].

articleTitle: Biological dielectrics in electric and magnetic fields
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Biological systems use the same atoms and molecules as the physical sciences. It is therefore reasonable that extant physical processes should be capable of giving a quantitative account of the interactions between electromagnetic fields and biological dielectrics from zero frequency upwards. When the present work commenced in 1974, it had already been suggested by Frohlich that enzymes and other biological materials might possess a metastable state with high electric dipole moment [1]. Consequently the present work then commenced with dielectric measurements and the effects of strong electric fields. Measurements on the enzymes, lysozyme, trypsin and ribonuclease gave results which were greatly influenced by temperature, humidity and electric field [2]. The general pattern of the results resembled those for a moist ferroelectric powder such as barium titanate.

articleTitle: The simultaneous measurement of light and current pulses in liquid dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: It is well established that light pulses are emitted during prebreakdown in liquid dielectrics [1,2,3]. These light pulses have been associated with the growth of negative streamers under divergent field conditions. Several attempts have been made to measure current pulses associated with the streamer growth. In two cases, current and light observations were correlated, however, in the case of Nelson, dc voltages were used[2,4]. Yamashita used transformer oil and 5 mm gaps under impulse conditions. To correlate streamer growth, light emission, and current pulses, it is of interest to use simple liquids to examine, simutaneously, the emission of light and prebreakdown current under non-uniform field conditions. In the following section, the experimental conditions used for this study are described. This is followed by a presentation of the results. In the last section, the significance of these results is discussed.

articleTitle: Maxwell-wagner effect and strong low-frequency dispersion
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The dielectric properties of dipolar materials are well understood in terms of the “universal” many-body approach developed by the Chelsea Group [1–4], with the characteristic power-law frequency dependence of the complex susceptibility above the loss peak frequency ω<inf>p</inf> given by: X(ω) = ∊(ω) − ∊<inf>∞</inf> ∝ [1 + i cot(nπ/2)] ω<sup>n−1</sup> (1) where the exponent falls generally in the range 0 < n < 1.

articleTitle: The effect of impurities on positive streamer propagation in n-hexane
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Recent studies [1–3] have shown that for electrical breakdown to occur a streamer must be initiated at one of the electrodes and travel to the opposite electrode to establish a conducting path. Of particular interest in this study are point-plane electrode geometries that produce convergent fields. That is, this work was limited to that case in which the point was the anode and the plane was the cathode. Under this condition, the streamer is initiated at the positive point and spreads toward the cathode [1, 4, 5, 6]. Recent studies [7, 8] have indicated that, for these positive streamers, at least three distinct modes of propagation can be identified. It appeared, therefore, desirable to investigate the influence of experimental parameters on these propagation modes. A descriptive list of the parameters which could affect breakdown measurements was compiled by Gallagher [9] and includes test procedure, material or surface state of the electrodes, electrode geometry, physical purity of the liquid (i.e., particle content), chemical purity of the liquid, temperature and hydrostatic pressure, and voltage duration. Previous investigations [1, 3] have suggested that the first two parameters can be controlled sufficiently well so that the measurement results could easily be replicated. This work investigates some effects of electrode spacing and chemical purity of the liquid. The fluid was filtered to minimize variations in the physical purity of the liquid as the other parameters were changed. The effects of temperature, pressure, and voltage duration will be investigated in future experiments.

articleTitle: Study of unusual conduction in FEP film
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: In the dielectrics the current decays with time to steady state. The absorbing current can be caused either from relaxation process of dipole or transport process of space charge. Common point of view is that leakage current is characterized by the steady state. And in some dielectrics unusual conductive phenomenon is observed, i.e., change of current with time is an increasing function. This phenomenon was observed in the ceramic materials (Ref.1). In our work we have observed unusual conduction in FEP film. For the polymer as insulant, studies of movement, trapping and disappearance of heterocharge, introduced during production processing and of homocharge, transferred from the metal, will be of value, because they have influence on the dielectric properties.

articleTitle: Analysis of antioxidant in aged cables
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Successful application of polyolefins as insulating materials for solid dielectric cable depends on their long-term stability against oxidation and electrochemical degradation. The usual method of stabilization is the addition of small quantities of antioxidants (AO), which act as radical scavengers in the oxidation process. The effectiveness of antioxidants depends not only on its capability for resonance stabilization but also on physical factors such as solubility, diffusivity, and volatility. The possibility of excess anti-oxidants accumulating and crystallizing in the voids and at interfaces of solid dielectric cable and acting as stress enhancers is important from service-life considerations.

articleTitle: Effects of hydrostatic pressure on water treeing properties of polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Water treeing is associated with high electric stress and contaminated environment involving moisture, water or chemical solutions. It is generally accepted that water trees cause reduction in breakdown voltage of cables, and currently suspected that water trees lead to final failure and decrease in the lifetime of cables [1]. A considerable amount of experimental data on water treeing is now available in the literature. These data have provided some important information bearing on the factors influencing the treeing properties as well as a clue to the possible mechanisms responsible for the initiation and the growth of water trees [2, 3], Although there is still no proper model generally accepted for these mechanisms, certain basic experimental facts seem to indicate that water treeing involves a forced penetration process. The main aim of the present paper is to present some new results related to this process.

articleTitle: Positive and negative lightning impulse breakdown of rod-plane gaps in nitrogen
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The breakdown characteristics of rod-plane gaps in nitrogen and N<inf>2</inf>-SF<inf>6</inf> mixtures are being studied by the authors, [1]. Some preliminary results on the breakdown characteristics of these gaps in pure nitrogen, as a function of rod diameter, gap spacing, gas pressure, and polarity of the applied impulse voltages are presented in this paper.

articleTitle: Time domain dielectric spectroscopy of plant stems
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Measurement of the dielectric properties of biological materials is important for many reasons. One in particular is the comparison of the properties of living systems with each other and with inorganic materials. Such studies can lead to a better understanding of the various conduction and polarization processes in living systems exposed to applied fields and perhaps to the development of models for non-thermal electromagnetic bioeffects. Unfortunately the in-vivo determination of the dielectric properties of biomateriale is often complicated by electrode effects. This paper describes two time-domain methods used to eliminate the contribution from electrodes and then obtain the intrinsic dielectric properties of plant stems.

articleTitle: Charge injection and transport analysis and measurements in highly purified water
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Because of its high dielectric constant, low cost, and ease of handling and disposal, water and water mixtures are being actively investigated for use as the dielectric in pulse power capacitors, pulse forming and transmission lines, and switches [1]. Recent charge injection analysis, terminal voltage-current measurements and Kerr electro-optic field mapping measurements have shown significant space charge effects on the electric field distribution [2,3]. Recent measurements for a water/ethylene glycol capacitor with stainless steel electrodes found that open circuit high voltage decay curves had a dielectric relaxation time that decreased with increasing initial voltage at room temperature, while at −10° C, the open circuit voltage decay had a negative second derivative with time in contrast to the expected exponential decay which always has a positive second derivative [2,3]. The decay rate also depended on the electrode spacing unlike a pure ohmic dielectric with conductivity σ and permittivity ε which has a dielectric relaxation time τ =ε/σ independent of geometry and voltage. These results indicated that the charge transport time of order ℓ<inf>2</inf>/(μV<inf>0</inf>) was also an important parameter. It was hypothesized that this anomalous behavior was due to positive space charge injection with density q that increases the ohmic conductivity σ to σ + qμ.

articleTitle: Physical mechanisms for the electret behavior of PETP
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Thermally-stimulated discharge (TSD) currents of polyethyleneterephtha-late (PETP) electrets were measured by a number of authors [e.g. 1–10]. Both, open-[6,9,10] and short-circuit [1–8] TSD arrangements were utilized. For samples charged above the glass-transition temperature T<inf>g</inf>, the TSD response consists of a dipole-deorientation peak around ? (“heterocharge”) and a space-charge peak at a higher temperature T (“homocharge”) which are opposite in sign (e.g. Fig. 3) [1,4,5]. In contrast, a typical open-circuit TSD response of corona-charged PETP exhibits two peaks of the same sign (Fig. 1). Conflicting interpretations of these responses include a two-trap space-charge model [9], a four-trap space-charge model [2], and a dipole-deorientation model [3,4,7,8] in addition to the above-mentioned dipole + space-charge model [1,4,5]. Recently, a new interpretation for the TSD response (Fig.1) of samples charged at room temperature (RT) was suggested [10]: the first peak at T<inf>g</inf> is attributed to the orientation of dipoles in the field of the trapped charges, whereas the second peak is thought to originate from detrapping of the charges. In the present study, this qualitative model [10] and the previous dipole+space-charge model [1] are combined, further refined, and supported by several experimental results.

articleTitle: Corona poling of polyvinylidenefluoride
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: A variety of charging techniques may be used for poling polyvinylidene-fluoride (PVDF) in order to obtain the desired piezoelectric [1] or pyroelectric [2] properties. The classical thermoelectret-forming method [3] requires heating of the sample. With this technique, local breakdown at a weak sample spot or at the electrode edges short-circuits the poling electrodes and thus prevents further poling. This effect is avoided by employing electrodes with a relatively high resistance distributed over the whole sample area: local breakdown then draws its current only from a small portion of the electrode area and therefore cannot short-circuit the whole electrode.

articleTitle: Area and time dependence of the breakdown of water under long term stress
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: If high dielectric constant fluids like water could be made to support electric stress for times approaching a millisecond, it should be possible to charge megajoule pulsed power systems directly from rapidly discharging mechanical devices. The limit on allowable stress times comes from the relatively low resistivity of high dielectric constant fluids. Resistivity may be increased by improving the purity of the fluid and by cooling it. This paper reports on the breakdown strength of water purified to its intrinsic resistivity level, then chilled nearly to freezing. Pulses of several hundred microseconds duration were applied to electrode areas of 80/ 400, 2000/ and 10/000 cm<sup>2</sup>. Small samples showed a “hysteresis” effect where the strength of the sample depended strongly on previous pulses. A typical lowering of the dielectric strength with increased area (area effect) was also observed. These data are used to demonstrate the applicability of the statistical model of area effects.

articleTitle: A piezoelectric effect in high voltage power capacitors
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: As part of a recent EPRI supported study∗, several hundred capacitors in service were monitored with a ∼70 kHz acoustic waveguide corona probe and meter. Numerous capacitors were found with very high and steady acoustic readings which were uncharacteristic of internal corona (PD) or arcing, and it was hypothesized that power line harmonics caused these acoustic emissions.

articleTitle: Proximity effect of a conducting plane in electro-optic field probe measurements
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Electric stresses are of critical importance in high voltage apparatus. Their measurement can be valuable, especially in situations where calculations are approximate, such as in three dimensional geometries or when transient impedances are not well known. This paper presents results of a study which examined the use of an electro-optic field probe for field measurements.

articleTitle: D.C. conductivity of ethylene propylene rubber
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: In recent years ethylene propylene rubber (EPR) has emerged as an important competitor of polyethylene as a high voltage cable insulator [1–6]. A survey of 120 utilities by R. L. Engsign [4] shows that 11% of them primarily use EPR for their insulation. In spite of its rising importance as an insulator, information on many aspects of EPR continues to be scanty compared to polyethylene. Like most polyethylenes now used for insulation EPR is crosslinked, but unlike polyethylene solid fillers are added to it during the manufacturing process [7].

articleTitle: On the velocity of positive streamer propagation in dielectric liquids
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The onset and propagation of discharge channels in insulators is of prime concern. The manner and rate of propagation of discharges is an important guide to the physical mechanisms involved. Most reports relating to discharge phenomena are only able to quote mean velocities for the discharge streamer. This can disguise the fact that the tip velocity is rarely constant with growth across the gap.

articleTitle: Ionization and attachment and breakdown measurements in SF6-CO2-air
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Electronegative gases, those which have the ability to attach free electrons and form stable negative ions include SF<inf>6</inf>, CO<inf>2</inf> and air and so on. These gases have numerous applications, including use as insulation for high voltage equipment, as donors in excimer lasers, and as scavengers in physical-chemical systems. Mixtures of SF<inf>6</inf> and other common gases are suitable for applications where low ambient temperatures could result in liquification of SF<inf>6</inf> if operated at higher pressures [1,2,3]. The use of a mixture of SF<inf>6</inf> and an inexpensive inert gas could eliminate some of the problems associated with pure SF<inf>6</inf> and reduce the insulation cost.

articleTitle: Accelerated aging to estimate life of short cable assemblies
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: In many practical apparatus, high voltage cables in the 10 to 50kV range are needed between modules. Such cables, in contrast to carefully designed coaxial lines with stress cones to minimize stress enhancements, may contain multiple wires, non-coaxial connectors, localized stress enhancements and non-homogeneous potting. Even with such short comings from the ideal, long life amounting to 5 to 10 or more years of operation is often desired. This paper considers practical cable assemblies and short time accelerated testing which can be employed to increase confidence that a particular design is adequate for needed service.

articleTitle: Conductivity mechanisms in complex fluids
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The present paper describes the results of a study of the electrical conductivity of residual petroleum oils. These oils are chemically complex mixtures and the particular type chosen for the study consisted of about 70% aromatic hydrocarbons, one half of which are PNA's (polynuclear aromatics) containing mostly 2 to 7 fused rings, 25% heterocyclic aromatic molecules (usually polar molecules containing nitrogen and oxygen), and the remainder aliphatic compounds. This liquid is almost black in color and highly viscous (η > 10,000 cps at 20°C), typical of a tar-like substance. The oil was mixed with a number of aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbon solvents, which allowed us to probe the mechanism of conductivity in these complex liquids.

articleTitle: Negative charge transport in FEP by constant current method
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Using the constant current triode<sup>1,2</sup>, we have been able to inject negative carriers in 12µm Teflon FEP foils, when the deposited charge density surpassed 2,3×10<sup>−7</sup>C/cm<sup>2</sup> (corresponding to 1,1 MV/cm). This is shown in curve I Fig.1. Initially the surface potential increases linearly with time. The linear behavior lasts until the voltage reaches a value of approximately 1400V. The subsequent sublinear growth of voltage with time indicates charge injection. We have verified that no potential decay is observed if the corona is cut off before the potential reaches V<inf>s</inf>, in dependently of the charging current I<inf>0</inf>. For long charging times, the voltage reaches a stationary value.

articleTitle: An investigation of the electrical ageing in low density polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The electrical ageing effects in low density polyethylene (LDPE) may be related to an accumulation of electronic and ionic space charges in the bulk. A study of thermally stimulated discharge currents (TSDC), in which the sample is short circuited through an electrometer as its temperature is increased at a steady rate from sub-zero temperature to a few degrees below its melting point, have shown two unexpected results [1,2], The first is that the largest currents were obtained with the virgin samples (uncharged) and the second, that all samples produced a TSDC peak at the same temperature irrespective of the type and field of charging. Now the total charge released in a conventional TSDC experiment may not correspond to the actual trapped space charges due to a cancellation of a part of the charges flowing in opposite electrodes and recombination of ionic species. Furthermore, the observed current is the algebraic sum of the flow of charges of both polarities towards both electrodes in the existing internal field and, therefore, can lead to false conclusions regarding the polarity and the spatial location of the majority carriers.

articleTitle: A study of electrical discharges growing in short confined gaps
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: In this work the authors attempt to characterise the electrical discharges initiated in hollow filaments of small diameter (a few microns) in a dielectric medium (low density polyethylene). Such discharges exist in the channels of electrical trees. Treeing is a degradation mechanism which affects solid insulators when they are subjected to local electric stresses close to their dielectric strength (a few MV/cm). The resulting tree takes the form of fine hollow channels, branching and interconnecting with one another. Much has been written on this subject /1/. The tree channels are filled with a gas whose principal component is hydrogen. Their diameter can vary from a few microns to some tens of microns. We have tried to explain how the discharge is affected by the proximity of the dielectric walls. Observation of the discharges initiated inside tree channels viewed through a light intensifier show that these discharges are localised randomly in the channels. Their initiation is therefore governed by parameters which we could not control. For this reason we have developed a system allowing a single discharge to be studied in a simulated tree channel.

articleTitle: Accelerated aging of XLPE cable insulation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The latest results of a continuing study into the deter ioration of cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE) insulation subjected to electric stress in the presence of water are described. Earlier results have shown that the breakdown strength of electrically aged XLPE was dependent on the amount of moisture in the insulation [1]. Temperature cycling has now been used to enhance water diffusion into the insulation and its effect on the breakdown strength and times to breakdown of miniature cables has been examined. Also the effect of fregency on the times to breakdown has been studied and is reported.

articleTitle: Charge accumulation on conical spacer in compressed SF6 gas at DC stress
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Surface charging phenomena on spacers have been investigated by several researchers<sup>(1–5)</sup> as collected charges may work to impair the flashover properties at the time of polarity reversal. Some charging mechanisms have been proposed, assuming gas phase<sup>(2,3)</sup> epoxy bulk <sup>(4)</sup> or surface<sup>(1)</sup> conduction in interpreting the charge accumulation. The authors have studied surface charging phenomena using a model cylindrical spacer placed between parallel electrodes with fine finish surface in compressed SF<inf>6</inf> gas and have indicated the possibility that surface charging is caused by electrical conduction on the surface of spacer.

articleTitle: Accelerated aging of high voltage machine insulation under combined thermal and electrical stresses
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: An attempt has been made in this study, to evaluate systematically the effects of electro-thermal aging (electrical stress from 8.0 kV/mm to 13.3 kV/mm and temperature from 70°C to 155°C) on a resin rich machine insulation system by measuring a number of electrical parameters. Results indicate that when the electric stress and temperature are both high, a breakdown of model samples is achieved very fast. The time to failure for any other situation depends upon the actual combination of electric and thermal stresses applied. The temperature developed in the system appears to play a more significant role in the deterioration of the insulation.

articleTitle: Considerations for valid accelerated life testing
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: For many situations, good estimates of the expected life of long-life materials, parts, or systems are essential. Practical considerations related to replacement costs, repair costs, maintenance costs, spare parts inventories, warranties, insurance, and safety all require good estimates of expected life. Unfortunately, such estimates are difficult to obtain. This is especially true for new systems when no field experience exists.

articleTitle: The current response of dielectric oil to steadily varying high voltage in a uniform crossed magnetic field
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The current flow through a test cell containing dielectric fluid has been investigated by steadily increasing and decreasing the applied voltage in recurring cycles from ground potential to levels well within the high field regime at a rate of one every 10 s [1]. After separating the displacement current from the charge transport component the latter was plotted logarithmically showing a sharply defined linear portion in the upper high field regime, the reciprocal slope s<sup>−1</sup><inf>u</inf> of which increased linearly with gap separation. Upon application of a crossed magnetic field to the cell the functional form of the variation of s<sup>−1</sup><inf>u</inf> with gap separation assumed a graphical form which lay concave to the abscissa. This particular testing technique of ramp voltage application was introduced initially by Seeker and Hilton for the purpose of measuring the breakdown voltage and they also investigated the influence of a crossed magnetic field [2]. The breakdown voltage of spherical brass electrodes was observed to increase by up to 4% with increasing flux density and then declined to below the usual breakdown value at 0.02 T for gap separations of 100 and 150 µm in purified and filtered hexane. By contrast the current response data of Watson and Girgis was obtained with copper electrodes in dimethyl siloxane in the gap range 0.6–1.4 cm. but breakdown data was not collected because of the tedious necessity of cleaning out the system after each rupture. In subsequent work, it was recognized that the threshold current and voltage above which the log-arithmic characteristic was linear was indeed a characteristic of the system which varies with ramp rate and impurity level of the oil [3]. This work has therefore been directed towards an investigation of the variation of the manner in which the threshold point varies with the crossed magnetic flux density. In addition variation of s<sup>−1</sup><inf>u</inf> with magnetic flux density has been further examined with gap separation over a range of magnetic flux densities and electrode materials.

articleTitle: The transport of low energy electrons in polystyrene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: This is a continuation of earlier work (1, 2) in which an electron injection technique was used to study the transport of charge carriers in thin films of polystyrene. In these studies an electron beam is used to inject charge into the free surface of the polymer film, and a higher energy beam monitors the surface potential of the film. From the time dependence of the surface potential and its variation with temperature one should be able to distinguish between the various possible transport mechanisms in the polymer. In our work using a 2 keV beam for charge infection we consistently observe currents which decay as t<sup>−1</sup> and this leaves an ambiguity of interpretation, as both trap-modified space-charge-limited tranpsort and beam-induced conductivity with bimolecular recombination can give rise to this same form of current decay. Repeating these charge decay measurements with low energy electrons (which should eliminate the contribution due to beam-induced conductivity) we observe charge decay characteristics which are similar to those using the 2 keV electrons. Thus we are able to distinguish between these two charge decay mechanisms: we conclude that beam induced conductivity effects are second order, and we are indeed observing electron transport in polystyrene, with electron mobility and range determined by the distribution of electron traps.

articleTitle: Effect of screens on oil gap flashover
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The conduction current and the breakdown voltage of a liquid can be considerably affected by placing an insulating barrier at one or both of the electrodes [1]. Similar effects have been observed in air and carbon tetrachloride [2,3]. These effects can be attributed to the distribution of space charges. It was found that the breakdown voltage of n-hexane depends on the availability of positive ions which in terms depend on the amount of oxygen dissolved in it and the nature of the anode surface [4].

articleTitle: Electrostatic subtraction radiography
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: A simple on-line analog method for subtraction radiography using electrostatic imaging techniques is presented, Various electrostatic imaging methods have been proposed for radiography. The best known is xeroradiography which has gained widespread use in mammography[1] and is based on x-ray induced charge cancellation on a prepolarized photoconductive plate to form an electrostatic latent image of the object. Another technique referred to as Electron Radiography [2] or gas ionography [3] employs a gas in an electric field such that free charge carriers produced in the gas by the x-ray photons subsequently form the electrostatic latent image of the object.

articleTitle: Effect of ambient temperature and air cavities on the breakdown voltage of synthetic materials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Synthetic insulating materials are produced by many production processes such as extruding, moulding, heating, vulcanizing and cooling. Voids or moisture can be contained in these materials due to one or more of the production processes. In addition, they may contain a large number of liquid-filled cavities and small particles. Some of these cavitites may be produced under operating conditions as a result of thermal or chemical deterioration of the insulation. This may occur due to ambient temperature and discharges in voids and cavities. The aim of this work is to study the effect of these two factors, namely ambient temperature and air cavities on the breakdown voltage of polystyrene and polyvinyl chloride as synthetic materials.

articleTitle: Stable dielectrics with giant polarization
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Certain macromolecular solids of highly aromatized structure can exhibit giant polarization. The structures must be capable of providing long range electron orbital de-localization. This can result in the presence of electronic carriers able to range over long molecular domains and produce the giant polarizations characteristic of the nomadic polarization mechanism. Recent developments in the synthesis and characterization of such materials now make available a new and interesting class of very stable organic dielectrics having dielectric constants in excess of 100. A number of such materials will be described.

articleTitle: Conductive polymers
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: There has been considerable interest among chemists and physicists during the past ten years in electrically conductive organic compounds [1]. The possibility of conductive materials that are light weight, inexpensive and easily processed has been especially attractive. This paper will describe what makes these organic materials conductive, and their properties in general, as well as results of recent work.

articleTitle: Ageing characteristic of suspected impurities in composite materials
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Composite insulating materials are much in use in high tension insulation. They offer a balance of electrical and mechanical properties. In these materials sometimes, there are spots of recrystallization and separation in the components at isolated points in the system. These require special attention as they could be possible reasons for failure during the ageing process, particularly under humidity and dust contamination. In these experiments the response of a contaminated composite material subjected to voltage stressing and high humidity along with artificial contaminants has been studied. A test rig made by us to co-relate the discharge properties of the material under stressed condition with reference to degradation due to ageing has been discussed. It is possible to co-relate the leakage current with certain impurities. This paper deals with some important parameters derived out of the investigation for the safe working life of such composite materials.

articleTitle: Ionically conducting polyether salt complexes
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Complexes of alkali salts and poly (ethylene oxide), (PEO)n·MX, are the most prominent members of a relatively new class of ionically conducting solids, the socalled polymer electrolytes [1, 2]. Although their conductivities are rather modest (10<sup>−6</sup>(Ωcm)<sup>−1</sup> or less at roomtemperature) these materials have met with considerable interest because of their potential use in batteries. In contrast to inorganic solid ionic conductors, these materials can be easily cast into thin flexible films.

articleTitle: Fine-structure in the dielectric gamma relaxations of high- and low-density polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: A perusal of the dielectric literature indicates that the γ transition, lying near −130°C/100 kHz, is made up one |1–4|, two |5, 6| or three |6| components, depending on prior treatment, extent of branching and instrument sensitivity. Similar results were found for dynamic mechanical |7–15| and NMR 116–18| studies. Dielectric studies generally favor amorphous sources and dynamic mechanical studies, both amorphous and crystalline sources. A study supporting the former point of view involves the lack of change in the shape of the dielectric loss tangent with increasing pressure |2|, while the existance of an unresolved dynamic mechanical loss for single crystal mats 119 I supports the latter point of view.

articleTitle: Material considerations for high frequency, high power capacitors
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Dielectric materials chosen for use in this high frequency, high power capacitor must endure hard vacuum conditions, high currents (up to 125 A rms), and frequencies up to 40 kHz. Temperature requirements for this type of capacitor are that capacitor operation must be efficient up to 125°C. A more stringent requirement for the solid dielectric is that the temperature coefficient of dissipation factor should indicate self stabilization well below 125°C. In addition, the dielectric temperature coefficient of capacitance should be negative.

articleTitle: Surface charging of insulators in a surface discharge switch
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Surface charging of insulators in a 45 kV, triggered surface discharge switch has been studied after repeated discharges. Static electric field measurements on different insulators such as G-10, Delrin and Lucite are compared. Electric fields as high as 10 kV/cm have been measured after several hundred discharges. These measurements also indicate long surface charge decay times. Decay times ranging from one hour to several hours for the charge to decay 10 percent have been measured. Utilizing the field measurements the influence of multiple insulator interfaces and placement of the trigger electrode are discussed.

articleTitle: Studies of the contact between metal and plasma-polymerized organosilicon films
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The use of thin plasma-polymerized organosilicon films as passive elements in electronic devices of MIS and MIM-type [1] needs the knowledge of the contact structure with metals. In the case of low surface state density this depends both on dielectric energy structure and the kind of metal, while in the case of high surface state density it depends only on the energy structure of silicon glass [2]. A very covenient method of M-I contact studies is the photoinjection of carriers from the electrode into the dielectric [3]. The results of energy structure investigation of organosilicon glasses [4,5] and their conductivity [6,7] as well as on photo-injection [8] made it possible to determine the structure of the metal-dielectric contact. Adaption of thermal current transient (TCT) [9,10] for M-I contact determination makes it possible to estimate the width of the depletion layer under different conditions of contact formation [11].

articleTitle: Induced loss characteristics in glass optical fibers under gamma radiation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: This paper reports the results of experiments concerned with the effects of drawing condition and OH content on radiation induced optical absorption bands in pure silica core fibers, especially a loss peak at 770nm under gamma radiation. The 770 nm band decreased under exposure to gamma radiation exceeding 10<sup>2</sup> Gy at room temperature. Radiation hardening also took place in the 770 nm band at room temperature.

articleTitle: Computing of electric field of skew conductors with various shapes of cross sections
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: In high voltage equipment, various arrangements of electrodes, which can have various shapes, are often used. Electrical insulation can be properly designed, and the best position can be chosen only if the electric field around the electrodes can be analysed. Skew conductors are those in arbitrary positions from which “special” positions (parallel, coaxial, eccentric, etc.) can be obtained. Therefore, equations for computing electric fields of skew conductors can be used for various concrete arrangements of conductors. In solving the fields in three dimensional regions by finite element models or finite difference methods, the number of equations is very large. Using a method of secondary sources, charge density on the conductors (i.e. in two dimensional regions) is calculated so the number of equations is reduced (1). From the known charge density, potential and intensity of the electric field at any point can be computed.

articleTitle: A theoretical approach for Townsend's first ionization coefficient in mixtures of gases
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Estimation of breakdown voltages of mixtures of gases is usually done empirically due to the incomplete knowledge of the fundamental phenomena which give rise to breakdown in gaseous mixtures. In this paper it is shown that the first ionization coefficient in gaseous mixtures can be obtained theoretically with special reference to electronegative gases and their mixtures with ordinary gases. The calculated values of ∝/p (first ionization coefficient/pressure) according to the developed equation and the values existing in literature are in good agreement. This equation can be used in determining the current growth and in understanding the behaviour of Swarm coefficients in mixtures of gases.

articleTitle: Bound water in aqueous mono-and disaccharide solutions: A depolarization thermocurrent study
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: We report in this paper on the dielectric behaviour of frozen aqueous solutions of mono-and disaccharides studied by the depolarization thermocurrent (DTC) method in the temperature range of 85–250 K and over a wide range of concentrations (0.0003–1.5 mol/l), to obtain information on the state of water in the solutions. The dielectric behaviour of aqueous oligosaccharide solutions was studied systematically by Tait et al.[1] and by Sugget and Clark [2] at temperatures of 5 and 25 C in the GHz frequency range. The main problem with such measurements is that the analysis of the measured frequency dependence of the complex permittivity in terms of contributions of free (bulk) water, hydration (bound) water and solute can never be completely unequivocal. We pointed out in a previous paper [3] that one may avoid such problems in the analysis of the measurements by using the DTC method. We showed in that paper that in frozen aqueous solutions of glucose there is a continuous transition from hydration to free H<inf>2</inf>O molecules. In this paper we extend our measurements to other monosaccharides and to disaccharides.

articleTitle: Design criteria for low frequency RF phantoms used in clinical NMR imaging and tumor hyperthermia
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Theoretical prediction of the SAR of RF energy by biological systems in the near field is difficult due to the nonorthogonality of electric E and magnetic H vectors and the propagation velocity changes at any dielectric discontinuity of complex geometries, though some specific cases have been evaluated [1,2,3]. For this reason, the use of phantoms of known geometry to approximate the specific absorption rate (SAR) of biological systems has facilitated the evaluation of mathematical models and has enabled calibration, standardization and normalized comparison of clinical and diagnostic instruments.

articleTitle: Analysis of combined electrical and thermal stress ageing of capacitor and rotating machine insolation systems
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Models for the analysis of failure of insulation subjected to synergy have now been put forward. These models invariably make use of Eyring relation in one form or the other. The Eyring model is based on physicochemical interaction of reactants of which the materials are composed. This model is found to be versatile since there is a provision in it by which the effects of two stresses of different nature acting simultaneously can be taken account of. Further, in the degenerate form, that is when one of the stresses is absent, it gives the corresponding single stress model. The Eyring equation is empirical in nature, from which the Arrhenius equation for thermal life can be evolved.

articleTitle: Study of DC conduction in aged transformer oil under non-uniform high fields
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: This paper emphasises experimental results of DC conduction current in aged transformer oil using point-plane configuration. The effects of oil dehydration and filtration, anode material and field strength are investigated and discussed. It is found that i-t and i-E characteristics display exponential “behaviour and tunneling phenomenon, respectively. Moreover, sample preparation and anode/liquid interface play an important role in explaining the mechanism of DC conduction under non-uniform high field.

articleTitle: Picosecond relaxations in proteins and biopolymers observed by MM-wave spectroscopy
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Broadband absorption measurements at millimeter wave frequencies are reported for several biological materials (lyophilized haemoglobin and lysozyme, silk keratin, poly-L-alanine). The measurements were extended over the temperature range from 4.2 K to 300 K using the oversized cavity technique. The millimeter wave absorption of the dry materials was found to increase nearly exponentially with temperature and as v…v<sup>2</sup> with frequency. This frequency and temperature dependence is described by picosecond relaxation processes in asymmetric double well potentials. These processes are assigned to the NH‖OC hydrogen bonds of the peptide backbone. For lysozyme the influence of hydration was investigated. The contribution of adsorbed water can be distinguished from the intrinsic processes by its different frequency dependence.

articleTitle: Thermal endurance test method for polimeric materials under closed circumstance
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: In thermal endurance tests of polymeric materials, Paavo Paloniemi presented the theory of equalized aging processes (EAP) (1). This paper applies EAP theory but changes the detection method for chemical reaction rate to gas chromatography and aims at the thermal endurance evaluation under closed circumstance.

articleTitle: Dielectric behaviour of proteins and their constituents
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Protein molecules contain numerous hydrophilic groups and in their natural state bind a great number of water molecules [1]. Their ionic character ensures that they are even more strongly polar than water; they display macromolecular dielectric relaxation in solution [2]. Proteins can be studied in the relatively dry polycrystalline state under controlled humidity [3]; they can be cast as films or glasses by evaporation from aqueous solution [4]; and they can be deposited as Langmuir-Blodgett monolayers or multilayers [5], which show both linear and non-linear dielectric effects [6].

articleTitle: Parameters and limits of bipolar conduction theory with AC excitation
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Electric fields and bipolar charge density distributions along with terminal currents for conduction between parallel plate electrodes have been theoretically defined by using a drift dominated conduction model which utilizes Langevin recombination and sinusoidal excitation. [1, 2] Charge carrier velocities in the model are proportional to the electric field through their mobilities. In return the electric field is also related to carrier charge densities through Gauss's law. Previous studies have compared terminal current waveform solutions from the model to measured waveforms with good results. This study extends previous results by including spatial and temporal solutions of electric fields, charge densities and terminal current with variations in charge density mobilities and applied frequency. Also, computation of mobility and limits of agreement between measurement and theory are defined.

articleTitle: Variation in threshold parameters of current response to ramped high voltage in silicone oil with synthetic films
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The reproducible current responses to applied symmetrical time varying ramp functions in silicone oil have recently been the subject of investigations [1, 2, 3]. Analysis of the data has shown that the current response on a log-log scale, has displayed two linear portions which are sharply divided and obey power laws of the form I=kV<sup>S u,ℓ</sup> in the high field regime where su and S<inf>ℓ</inf> are the logarithmic slopes of the upper and lower sub-regimes respectively [1, 2]. The superimposition of the mean and differential current characteristic curves obtained from the current response loops has revealed common threshold points of intersection [1]. The threshold point parameters of voltage and current have been seen to vary accurately with the applied voltage ramp rate. The detailed analysis has unveiled a remarkable fact that the current was neither purely conductive nor displacement current, but instead it is a mixture of both components [1]. The logarithmic conductances at threshold points have analytically been determined to be less than unity value in oil only experiments. The experiments conducted with a single layer of thin film in different viscosities of oil furthermore, have indicated the magnitude of the conductance to be closer to unity as reported in an earlier paper [1]. The investigation and its findings presented here are a continuation of that work in which the influence upon the threshold parameteres of the variations in the applied voltage ramp rate, the number of thin layers of synthetic film employed within the composite dielectric and the impurities in oil have been studied.

articleTitle: Interface effects on electrical conduction in PE-EVA laminates
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: As most of practical insulation systems are composites of insulating materials and conductors, it is very important to understand interracial phenomena at dielectric-dielectric and dielectric-conductor interfaces in order to improve the insulating properties. Recently, thermally-stimulated current (TSC) techniques were applied to polymer-mica and polymer-oil systems [1–3] and proved powerful in these investigations.

articleTitle: Thermally activated processes in polymers below and above the glass transition
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Thermally activated transfigurations in the microstructure of amorphous matter are studied in the paper in order to derive the activation energies of the processes such as relaxation polarisation [1], plastic deformation etc.

articleTitle: A simple model of electron beam initiated dielectric breakdown
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: This paper describes a simple model of a beam charging experiment. The motivation for the model is the need to understand low voltage breakdown such as that which occurs in dielectric material exposed to the radiation environment of space [1]. Our approach to the problem is motivated by the work of O'Dwyer [2] on high voltage breakdown.

articleTitle: Tentative explanation of the influence of electric field on the activation energy for conduction in dielectrics
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Although the electrical properties of polyethylene (PE) have been measured by many authors, there is still no comprehensive theory able to fully describe the different phenomena observed. We have shown elsewhere (1) that the applied electric field, F, and pressure reduce the activation energy, E. We also observed that the existing theories do not provide a correct description of experimental results obtained under different conditions. In fact, the best fit to experimental data over a large range of fields is an exponential decrease of E with F, despite the fact that there is no theoretical support for such an empirical relation. Before entering into the discussion of the physical significance of this relation, an attempt was made to know whether it applies also to other materials.

articleTitle: Organic conductors for solar cells
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Solar cell is one of the most important components in solar energy based equipments as an alternate energy source. Conventional absorption type of collectors are massive and have maintenance problems. Solar cells do the same function of collection very precisely. Conventional solar cells, in general, based on silicon single crystals are MIS or SIS types which have received much attention recently but there is no particular material or combination available which is cheap enough to compete with the large scale fossil-fuel generated electricity.

articleTitle: Synergism factor in binary mixtures of electronegative and buffer gases
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Synergism effect is the rapid increase in the breakdown strength of gaseous mixtures with the addition of small percentage of electronegative gases (SF6, CCl<inf>2</inf>F<inf>2</inf>., etc.) to the buffer gases (N<inf>2</inf>, air, etc.). To understand this phenomenon, extensive analysis of the data have been made of the ionization and attachment coefficients (α and η) and the ratio of diffusion coefficient to mobility (D/µ) for electrons in mixtures of SF<inf>6</inf>-N<inf>2</inf> and CCl<inf>2</inf>F<inf>2</inf>-N<inf>2</inf> over a wide range of E/N(T<inf>d</inf>) (E is the electric field in Vm<sup>−1</sup>, N is the gas number density in m<sup>−3</sup> and 1 T<inf>d</inf> = 10<sup>−21</sup> Vm<sup>2</sup>). The investigations have resulted in empirical relationships which relate the attachment coefficient, the critical E/N (corresponding to α = η), the electron mean energy (∊) and the breakdown voltage of the mixture (V<inf>mix</inf>) respectively with those of its electronegative and buffer gas constituents and a common factor β, which is termed as “Synergism factor”.

articleTitle: Conductive polymers with very low temperature coefficient of resistivity
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Polymers with high dark conductivity obtained by specific synthesis and doping or by mixing with conducting fillers/necessary concentration of additives >20%/ exhibit deterioration of typical polymeric properties. A new method of making commercial polymers conductive by the addition of as little as 1 wt% of a conductive material has recently been elaborated.[1]. This method takes advantage of the fact that well conducting organic charge-transfer /CT/ complexes, the so called “organic metals”, are able to crystallize in the polymer matrix during film casting. The process consists in growing conductive CT complexes in correlated, somehow alligned crystallites forming a conducting network at such low additive content. This method is called reticulate doping. Our papers [1,2,3] describe the mechanism of the network formation, the conditions under which it can be formed, and the relationship between the morphology of the CT complex crystallites and the properties of the obtained materials. In the present communication another interesting property is discussed — an unusual temperature dependence of the electrical conductivity in reticulate doped polymers.

IEEE Keywords: Active matrix organic light emitting diodes

articleTitle: Influence of changes in the physical and chemical environment on the growth of water trees in polyolefins
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The complex phenomenon of water treeing has been extensively researched since first reported by Lawson and Vahlstrom over 10 years ago [1]. It is well documented that the environment near the treeing inception point plays a role in the treeing process and that some chemicals added to the system can supress initial tree growth [2–5], After years of studying the role of additives, however, the actual mechanisms responsible for water treeing are still not clear.

articleTitle: The performance of the perfluorocarbon liquid/plastic film capacitor technology in pulse power service — A current status report
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: At the 1982 CEIDP meeting, a paper by Mauldin, Nunnally, and Sarjeant was presented which described a program to evaluate the Sandia perfluorocarbon liquid/ plastic film capacitor technology in pulse power service [1].

articleTitle: Dielectric analysis and measurements of thermally evaporated erbium fluoride thin films
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Very high precision capacitors with good stability are required for the fabrication of thin film hybrid integrated circuits. Materials that warrant such attention include rare earth fluorides and oxides owing to their mechanical and chemical stability [1]. Erbium fluoride films have been studied with regard to its electroluminescence only [2]. This paper reports an investigation on the dielectric analysis and measurements of thermally evaporated erbium fluoride thin films.

articleTitle: Conduction and breakdown characteristics of thermally evaporated stearic acid films
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Thin films of organic fatty acids such as stearic acid (C<inf>17</inf>H<inf>35</inf>COOH), deposited by Langmuir-Blodgett technique have been widely investigated and the progress reviewed (1,2). However, very little is known about the conduction and breakdown characteristics of thin films of stearic acid deposited by thermal evaporation in vacuum. Agarwal and Mitsuhashi (3) have studied the high field conduction characteristics using a planar electrode geometry and Kasilingam et al (4,5) have reported the conduction and breakdown characteristics on sandwich electrode geometry. In these studies (3–5) the film deposition parameters were; pressure in the 10<sup>−5</sup> to 10<sup>−6</sup> Torr range and film deposition rate of −10Å/s. Moreover, no attempt was made to avoid the formation of an Al<inf>2</inf>O<inf>3</inf> film on the lower aluminum electrode prior to the deposition of the stearic acid film. In this paper we have reported breakdown behavior and dielectric nature of stearic acid films deposited at much lower pressure (∼10<sup>−8</sup> Torr) and at a much lower film deposition rate). We have also used proper masking and a dual source evaporator to deposit the lower Al electrode and the stearic acid film without disturbing the vacuum so that no oxide layer is formed between the lower electrode and the stearic acid film. Sandwich structures have capacitance/area ranging from 0.027 to 0.033 f/m<sup>2</sup>, the dielectric constant between 1.45 and 2.04, and DC breakdown field strength ranging from 9.27 × 10<sup>7</sup> to 7.63 × 10<sup>8</sup> V/m.

articleTitle: Eddy currents in human tissues and whole body nuclear magnetic resonance imaging
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The use of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) as a new method for developing diagnostic information on human patients is attracting great attention and gaining rapid acceptance at the present time [1],[2]. In this paper we will review the basic principles of this technique and describe how they can be used — in a noninvasive fashion — to extract information from the interior of the human body.

articleTitle: Correlation between structure change and dielectric property changes of polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: In the last few years results have been presented in which authors have cited infrared spectra as evidence of oxidation of polyethylene in cables. Thermal, electrical, water ageing, and multistresses have been used to produce oxidized elements in polyethylene. These elements could be found by using infrared spectra. Once the water has diffused into the polyethylene (PE), oxidation and com­bined mechanical stresses along weak paths seem to be the most likely mechanism for breakdown. Breakdown due to some type of oxidation has also been postulated.

articleTitle: Dielectric studies of artemia cysts using time domain spectroscopy
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: There exists today a great deal of controversy regarding the physical state of water in biological systems. A question is whether or not the water in these systems may be assumed to behave according to the fundamental postulates of dilute solution theory. The resolution of this controversy will help determine which of the basic theories of cellular function is more realistic.

articleTitle: Electrical phenomenology of the keratins of human skin
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The keratins may be loosely defined as those proteins containing sulfur in the form of cystine and cysteine. Adjacent molecules of cysteine tend to combine by cross-linking such that — SH groups are oxidized to — S-S groups and strong disulfide bonds are formed. Keratins may also be divided into two basic types, called hard or filamentous keratins and soft or amorphous keratins respectively. Filamentous or hard keratins are the major components of mammalian hairs, wools, claws, nails and quills, and constitute important biological polymers. Furthermore, the physiology of mammalian epidermis is designed to produce a tough, dead outer stratum of about twenty layers of flattened, interdigitated cells principally filled with a mixture of filamentous and amorphous keratins. In humans this part of the skin is called the stratum corneum, and it forms the principal barrier to the permeation of substances into the body [1]. Its permeability is however greatly affected by its degree of hydration.

articleTitle: Effects of nuclear radiation on the electrical properties of polyethylene
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983

articleTitle: Labyrinthine instability in dielectric fluids
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: A uniform magnetic field tangential to the interface between fluids of different magnetizability or a uniform electric field parallel to the interface between two different permittivity fluids is always stabilizing to small signal waves along the field, having no effect on interfacial waves transverse to the field [1]. However, recent work has demonstrated interfacial instability when magnetic fluid is confined with an immiscible nonmagnetic fluid between closely spaced parallel plates, with a uniform magnetic field applied normal to the plates and parallel to the thin dimension of the interface [2–4]. At a threshold field strength a comblike pattern develops which grows to a complicated labyrinth pattern of two simply connected but highly convoluted regions [5].

articleTitle: Langmuir-blodgett films in dielectric and biological research
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Since the pioneering work of Langmuir and Blodgett [1] in the early part of this century, the study of monomolecular layers floating on water or transferred onto solid substrates has been the realm of the physical chemist. The upsurge of interest in the properties of these films in recent years has seen Langmuir-Blodgett (LB) films emerge as a truly multidisciplinary subject in which molecular biologists, biochemists, chemists, physicists and even electrical/electronic engineers have, [2,3] and will, make important contributions.

articleTitle: A radiation induced foil electret
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Electrets have numerous practical applications in science, industry and medicine. Originally, they were produced through thermal (thermoelectrets)[1] or optical (photoelectrets)[2] charge deposition methods; in recent years, however, isothermal charge deposition techniques have been favored because of their simplicity and speed.

articleTitle: Optimization of the piezoelectric properties of uniaxially stretched polyvinylidene fluoride films corona poled at room and elevated temperatures
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Recent work has shown that corona poling of stretched polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) films at elevated temperature considerably enhances piezoelectric properties [1,2]. Some three dozen applications of field or corona poled PVDF films are listed in a recent paper by Sessler [3]. These may be classified under the general headings of audio frequency, ultrasonic, underwater and electromechanical transducers and devices. Many new applications are in the development stage.

articleTitle: Charge accumulation and filtration in insulating expansions filled with agitated dielectric liquids
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: In coolant loops for high voltage equipment or during fueling operations, flowing semi-insulating liquids acquire net charge where they contact potential-constrained metallic surfaces, as in heat sinks or metal tubes [1], and produce potentially hazardous charge accumulations at surfaces where the potential is free to rise, as in insulating tubes [2] or at free liquid surfaces in tanks [3]. This paper describes charge accumulation in an insulating expansion where liquid fills the available volume and is continuously exchanged through potential-constrained inlet and outlet tubes. The incoming liquid jet produces essentially random turbulent motions that obscure the mean flow and tend to uniformly distribute the resident volume charge. Given specified geometric and physical parameters and a known arbitrary inlet current, the model predicts a charging transient, and the associated field generation in the insulating expansion wall, that is largely insensitive to expansion shape. This transient leads to a stationary state in which the incoming convection current is balanced by ohmic leakage driven by the generated field. The model and supporting experiments prompt application of the expansion as a passive charge filter to protect downstream elements that are sensitive to electrical breakdown.

articleTitle: The use of holographic interferometry as a diagnostic tool for liquid & composite dielectric systems
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: Mechanistic explanations of breakdown in dielectric liquids have relied on fast Schlieren systems to study pre-breakdown streamers & the Kerr effect [1] to evaluate the field distribution. Holography has previously been used to suppress the incoherent light resulting from dielectric breakdown [2]. The present contribution describes the application of holographic interferometry to obtain an optical probe of greater sensitivity and indicates possible applications. The use of holography permits the detection of phase shifts in a stressed liquid which are only a small fraction of the wavelength of light & allows this increased sensitivity in spite of the inherent poor optical quality of the test liquid, enclosure & arbitrary interfaces present.

articleTitle: Anomalous polarization effects in low density polyethylene with A.C. charging
publicationTitle: Conference on Electrical Insulation & Dielectric Phenomena - Annual Report 1983
abstract: The presence of persistent polarization in electrically stressed (d.c.) low density polyethylene (LDPE) may be determined from an analysis of current transients arising from a step input of thermal radiations, incident on the polymer surface with its electrodes shorted. It has been shown [1–3] that for charging fields smaller than 4.0 × 10<sup>7</sup>V m<sup>−1</sup>, the current transients may arise from a presence of impurity ions and at fields greater than 4.0 × 10<sup>7</sup>V m<sup>−1</sup> injected space charges become the dominant contributors in influencing the non-uniform polarization in a complex manner.
